Maladaptive Strategies.value: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
I think about why the event has happened to me
push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe

Threat.value: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert

Memory.value: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.

Negative Appraisals.value: The world is a dangerous place
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power

vignette: At seventy‑six, Samuel—an Anglo‑American man who has spent most of his adult life behind the register of a suburban grocery store—recalled the night he fled a shell‑hit village in the war zone where he had lived as a civilian. The blast had torn through the narrow street, sending glass and splinters flying, and the air was thick with the acrid smell of burning. He could still see the flash of the mortar, hear the shrill cries of his neighbors, and feel the ground shudder beneath his feet. Those images now resurface in his mind as stark, monochrome photographs, a visual memory he can pull at any time. Each time he does, his thoughts drift to the belief that the world is a dangerous place and that he has lost the faith he once had in people, in life, and in a higher power. The starkness of those memories feeds his conviction that he is no longer capable of the roles that defined him—of being a reliable cashier, of being a pillar for his community. In turn, these negative appraisals sharpen the vividness of the memories, making the recollections feel almost as real as the night itself. He wakes at night, the echo of distant artillery fire ringing in his ears, as if the danger is still looming, and he lies in a bed that feels too small, too quiet to keep his guard down. The persistent threat that hangs over him—his hypervigilance, his watchful gaze at anyone who crosses the store’s threshold—has pushed Samuel toward a series of avoidance strategies. He has stopped driving, both out of fear that a sudden collision could resurrect the shock of that war night and because being in a vehicle feels like a cramped, controlled environment where any noise could trigger the memory. When he is a cashier, he finds himself watching customers’ faces closely, looking for signs that they might pose a danger, and once an interaction ends he instinctively pushes away any positive emotions that might surface, believing that happiness feels unsafe and could be exploited. He can no longer sit quietly at home after a long day; the stillness feels like a threat, and he is compelled to keep his mind busy, to keep his attention turned outward. Samuel’s constant state of alertness reinforces his belief that the world is unsafe and that he is powerless. The idea that he must remain vigilant at all times erodes his confidence that he can navigate daily life without being harmed. As his avoidance deepens, the cycle of threat and withdrawal tightens: the more he avoids driving, the less he is able to see the outside world and the more isolated he feels. This isolation, in turn, heightens his sense of danger, feeding back into his hypervigilance and his need to suppress any positive feelings that might make him vulnerable. The cycle grows more rigid; the less he engages with people, the more he believes the world is a place of harm, and the more he believes he cannot cope with it. The very strategies that Samuel adopts—avoidance of driving, suppression of joy—serve to keep his memories alive. By keeping his mind in a constant state of readiness, the recollection of the night’s violence stays vivid, as if it could flare to life at any moment. His isolation and avoidance also reinforce his belief that he is incapable of the roles he once valued, further cementing his negative appraisal of himself and the world. He has stopped volunteering with his local community group, once a source of warmth and connection, because the thought of interaction now feels like stepping into a minefield. His work schedule has shifted: he no longer takes the early shift that would require him to drive to the store, instead working the late hours when the crowds thin and the threat feels less immediate. The routine has settled into a pattern that keeps his memories and appraisals entwined, each feeding the other in a self‑reinforcing loop that has left him increasingly isolated and numb. It was the cumulative weight of these symptoms—frequent night awakenings, a constant sense of impending danger, an inability to enjoy the small pleasures of a morning coffee or a friendly customer greeting—that finally pushed Samuel to seek help. He fears that if he does not address the cycle, his health will deteriorate further, and he might lose the one thing that still gives him purpose: his job at the store. Yet he also holds a flicker of hope that, perhaps, learning to trust his own safety once more could bring back the sense of normalcy he has long missed.
